newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Helicopter gunships patrol Uzbek-Afghan border.
newsitem.headline: Helicopter gunships patrol Uzbek-Afghan border.

text.p: Helicopter gunships patrolled Uzbekistan's border with Afghanistan on Thursday in a show of strength during a fierce tug of war over the nearby Afghan town of Mazar-i-Sharif.
The Soviet-built aircraft buzzed a stretch of the sluggish, biscuit-coloured waters of the Amu Darya River which mark the frontier between war stricken Afghanistan and its ex-Soviet neighbour.

Uzbek troops dug trenches at the frontier crossing after black-turbaned fighters of the fundamentalist Islamic Taleban militia, which seized the Afghan capital Kabul last year, marched into Mazar-i-Sharif 60 km (40 miles) away at the weekend.

The Taleban have since been repulsed from the town but Russia and a clutch of shaky ex-Soviet states in Central Asia still fear any northward spread of fundamentalist Islam towards their southern borders.
They worry that the Taleban's radical brand of Islam could provoke instability amid the ethnic groups which straddle remote mountain and desert frontiers.
The rapid collapse of the anti-Taleban alliance they had quietly backed sent a shiver of panic through the region.
On Thursday, border troops were tight-lipped on what steps had been taken to reinforce the frontier.
"We've strengthened the border regime," said an Uzbek officer, wearing mottled khaki combat fatigues and a floppy bush hat, a desert uniform unchanged since Soviet times.

"If before we had to patrol eight or ten hours a day, now we have to be on duty for up to sixteen hours," said the officer, who declined to be named, in charge of a command post about 18 km (12 miles) from the Uzbek border town of Termez.

A young conscript, a Kalashnikov assault rifle slung across his back, set off with a dog on a leash to patrol a fence of concrete and razor wire, broken up every at intervals by watchtowers on spindly legs.
The reeds on the banks of the Amu Darya River, or the Oxus, crossed by Alexander the Great and more recently by a doomed Soviet invasion force, gave way quickly to desert.
The baked outlines of old mosques and Buddhist temples were visible in the distance.
"We could hear the fighting at night when the Taleban went into Mazar-i-Sharif," said a non-commissioned officer at the command post. "It's quiet now."
There was no sign of refugees at the Friendship Bridge, a construction of metal girders about a kilometer (mile) long which forms the crossing -- now closed -- into Afghanistan.
Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, told a news conference in the Uzbek capital Tashkent on Thursday that she saw no imminent refugee crisis.
"Right now there is no movement of people but there is always the possibility that many women and children will need protection," she said.
About 10 United Nations staff wanting to escape the fighting in Afghanistan crossed the bridge on foot on Thursday, carrying few belongings, and were driven to a U.N. base in Termez.
